chunks: What a PCB is and where it's used. The question: What is a PCB? Name some applications.
A printed circuit board, or PCB, is a flat insulating board with copper conductors on it.
Components are soldered to pads on the board, and the copper traces connect them in the pattern the design requires.
It replaces a tangle of loose wires with something repeatable, compact and easy for machines to assemble.
PCBs range from a one-layer board in a remote control to a board with twenty layers in a server.
Picture a city map printed on a board. The streets are copper traces, the buildings are components, and the doors of the buildings are pads where the solder goes.
A via is a tunnel or ramp that takes a road from one level to another. Every board made from the same map has exactly the same streets, which is the whole point.
The analogy leaves out that streets here are not perfect: a trace has a little resistance, inductance and capacitance, and these matter at high speed.
A top view of a small board. Components (U1, R1) are soldered to orange pads.
Solid traces connect pads on the top layer; a via drops a signal to another layer (dashed), where it continues as a trace.
Mounting holes, board outline and silkscreen labels complete the picture. Soldermask covers everything except the pads.
Trace: a copper conductor on a PCB layer. Pad: exposed copper where a component lead is soldered. Via: a plated hole that connects copper on different layers.
FR-4: the common fiberglass-epoxy material that insulates and supports the copper. Soldermask and silkscreen: the protective coating over the copper and the printed labels on top.
A common board is FR-4, 1. 6 mm thick, with 1 oz copper, which is about 35 µm thick. That copper has about 0.
49 milliohms for every "square" of trace (a piece as long as it is wide). A trace 0. 25 mm wide and 50 mm long is 200 squares, so its resistance is about 200 times 0.
00049 equals 0. 098 ohms. The same trace on the outer layer carries roughly 0. 9 amps for a 10 degrees Celsius temperature rise. So a trace is a real conductor with real limits.
That is the whole idea.
"A PCB is an insulating board, usually fibreglass-epoxy FR-4, with copper traces etched on it that connect components soldered to pads.
Vias connect layers, soldermask protects the copper and silkscreen labels the parts.
We use them because they're repeatable, compact, machine-assembled and let you control impedance and return paths.
They're in everything from remote controls to servers, from a single layer up to twenty or more layers."
